kurals.tamil:
இகலென்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் பகலென்னும்
பண்பின்மை பாரிக்கும் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikalenba ellaa uyirkkum pakalennum
panbinmai paarikkum noi.
kurals.meaning: The wise call hostility a disease: in every living being it feeds the ugly trait of refusing to get along with others.
kurals.elementary: Think of a bad cold that spreads from one kid in class to everyone. Grudges work the same way: one person stops getting along with another, and soon nobody can play together. The poet says that kind of falling-out is a sickness, and it can catch anyone.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition: ikal (இகல், hostility, mental antagonism) is a noi (நோய், disease) that ‘spreads out’ or ‘nourishes’ (paarikkum, பாரிக்கும்) pakal (பகல், separation, non-union) in all creatures. The wordplay is deliberate: pakal normally means ‘daytime’ but here carries its older sense of ‘division’, which Puliyur Kesigan glosses as kūdāmai (கூடாமை, not coming together) and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘failing to harmonise with other lives’. The traditional commentators following Parimelazhagar treat ikal as the inner root from which outward enmity (pagai, the subject of the next chapter, Pagaimaatchi) grows, which explains why this chapter sits in the Natpiyal (friendship) section of Porutpal. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ikal unusually as ‘contempt’ (இகழ்ச்சி) that resists another’s nature; Kalaignar emphasises its social result, people unable to live together. The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire-turned-wrath as the one enemy that devours everything in the world.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise names a single inner disease, hostility, as the common affliction of all living beings.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good thematic parallel (an inner passion as universal enemy), though the Gita’s focus is lust-and-anger rather than discord specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points out that any household or realm torn by internal division destroys itself.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s pakal, disunion, is exactly the division Jesus says no house can survive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on disunion as destructive; Mark speaks of its effects rather than calling it a disease.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands unity and recalls how enemies were turned into brothers by God’s grace.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat division between hearts as the core danger and union as the remedy.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the disunion theme; framed theologically rather than as a disease.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Joshua said: an evil eye, the evil inclination, and hatred for humankind put a person out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists hatred of people (sinat ha-briyot) among the three traits that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the rabbis see hatred of others as a ruinous inner condition rather than a passing mood.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: hatred of fellow creatures as a destructive trait.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust and no crime like hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks hatred as the worst of wrongs, alongside lust as the worst fire.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts single out hostility as the gravest affliction of living beings.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Quoted the first half of the verse; matches the severity, not the disease image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eris, goddess of Strife, uninvited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, tossed a golden apple marked for the fairest among the guests, setting Hera, Athena and Aphrodite against each other and, through the Judgement of Paris, starting the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: One act of spiteful discord spread until it engulfed gods, heroes and whole cities.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth dramatizes the Kural’s idea that discord is a contagion that spreads to all.
greek_mythology.source: Eris and the Apple of Discord (Cypria, summarized by Proclus; Theoi)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative illustration of spreading discord, not a definition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Republic, Socrates argues that injustice breeds factions, hatreds and quarrels that make any group, and even a single soul, incapable of acting together and an enemy to itself.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that internal division paralyses both cities and individuals.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘disease that breeds disunion’ is the same diagnosis of self-defeating division.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Plato ties faction to injustice rather than to hostility as such.

kurals.tamil:
பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும் இகல்கருதி
இன்னாசெய் யாமை தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakalkarudhip patraa seyinum ikalkarudhi
innaasey yaamai thalai.
kurals.meaning: Even if someone, set on breaking with you, does things you dislike, the highest course is not to hurt them in return out of hostility.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a classmate stops being your friend and does mean little things to you. You could plan to get back at them, but the poet says the best thing is not to. Not paying back meanness with meanness is what a really strong person does.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a symmetry of motives: the other person acts pakal karudhi (பகல் கருதி, intending separation) and does patraa (பற்றா, unloving or disagreeable things), while you are warned against acting ikal karudhi (இகல் கருதி, out of hostility) and doing innaa (இன்னா, harmful things). The final word thalai (தலை, ‘head’, foremost) marks this restraint as the supreme course. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar both read it as forbearance under provocation; Solomon Pappaiah calls it a ‘superior quality’ (சிறந்த குணம்). The thought echoes the Aram chapters on Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314, but here it is set in Porutpal as practical statecraft: retaliation turns disagreement into lasting enmity. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant ... such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as without hatred (adveṣṭā), friendly and forgiving toward all.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural asks the same refusal of hatred even toward those who wrong us.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Excerpt with ellipsis; strong on non-hatred and forgiveness, less specific about provocation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers never to repay harm with harm.
christianity.tie_back: This is nearly a word-for-word restatement of the Kural’s counsel.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an permits equal retaliation but ranks pardon and reconciliation higher.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names restraint, not retaliation, as the better path.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: permits retaliation but prizes pardon, as the Kural prizes restraint.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart ... Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids both inner hatred and outward revenge.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly forbids acting on hostility even when provoked.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: no hatred, no vengeance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that letting go of the record of wrongs is how hatred ends.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise asks us not to let another’s offences become our motive to harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on not dwelling on injuries; less about outward retaliation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 24, Achilles, whose friend Patroclus was killed by Hector, receives Hector’s grieving father Priam, weeps with him, and gives back Hector’s body instead of continuing to dishonour it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest warrior finally sets aside his rage against an enemy who wronged him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles shows, late and at great cost, the restraint the Kural asks for from the start.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial fit: Achilles had already retaliated before relenting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Crito, Socrates argues that one must never do wrong, and therefore must never return wrong for wrong or do evil to anyone, whatever one has suffered from them.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates rejects retaliation as itself a form of wrongdoing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural reaches the same conclusion: provocation never licenses harm.

kurals.tamil:
இகலென்னும் எவ்வநோய் நீக்கின் தவலில்லாத்
தாவில் விளக்கம் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikalennum evvanoi neekkin thavalillaath
thaavil vilakkam tharum.
kurals.meaning: If you rid yourself of the painful disease called hostility, it will give you a renown that never fades and never fails.
kurals.elementary: Imagine carrying a heavy, smelly bag of grudges everywhere you go. When you finally drop it, you feel lighter, and people start to remember you as the kind one. The poet says letting go of hostility makes you shine in a way that lasts.
kurals.university: Evvanoi (எவ்வநோய்) is a compound of evvam (எவ்வம், distress, affliction) and noi (disease): hostility is a sickness that torments its host. Its removal yields vilakkam (விளக்கம், literally ‘light, clarity’, here ‘renown, distinction’) qualified twice: thaval illaa (தவல் இல்லா, undiminishing) and thaavil (தாவில், flawless or unfailing). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the outcome as imperishable fame (அழியாத புகழ்), Kalaignar as ‘stainless, lasting fame’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes vilakkam more literally as inner clarity. The image of illness and cure continues from 851, so the chapter treats hostility medically: diagnosis (851), restraint (852), cure and its fruit (853). Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Among the divine qualities (daivī sampad) Krishna lists in Gita 16.1-3 are freedom from anger, freedom from malice (adroha) and forgiveness, which he says lead toward liberation, while the demonic qualities bind.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats freedom from hostility as part of the radiant, divine nature.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural promises a lasting radiance (vilakkam) to those who remove hostility.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; links non-malice to a higher state, not specifically to fame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts a healthy heart with envy that rots a person from within.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts picture ill will as a disease and its absence as health and life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the disease image, but speaks of envy rather than hostility and does not mention fame.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who swallow their anger and forgive, calling them beloved of God.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises honour to those who rid themselves of hostile feeling.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on the reward for restraint; the reward is divine love rather than worldly renown.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What man is he that desireth life, and loveth many days, that he may see good? ... Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm promises long life and good to the one who leaves evil and actively pursues peace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly promises an unfading reward to those who put away hostility.
judaism._accuracy_note: Excerpt with ellipsis; reward is long life and good, not renown.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha declares that only the removal of hatred ends hatred, as a timeless law.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts present the removal of hostility as the one cure, with a lasting result.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the cure theme; the Kural’s stress on renown is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena persuades the vengeful Furies to give up their wrath against Athens; they become the Eumenides, ‘Kindly Ones’, and receive an honoured, permanent home and worship in the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Spirits of hostility, once they lay aside their anger, gain lasting honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s promise of unfading distinction to whoever casts out hostility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good structural parallel (wrath given up, lasting honour gained); paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca closes On Anger by urging that, since life is short, we should spend it not in hostility but in cultivating humanity, so that no one fears us and we leave a gentle memory.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that freedom from anger is the path to a calm life and a good name.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise links ending hostility with lasting good repute.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the close of De Ira; thematic rather than exact.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் பயக்கும் இகலென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inbaththul inbam payakkum ikalennum
thunbaththul thunbang kedin.
kurals.meaning: When hostility, the worst of all miseries, is destroyed, it yields the greatest of all joys.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever made up with a friend after a big fight? That warm, happy feeling afterwards is one of the best feelings there is. The poet says being angry at someone is the worst kind of unhappy, so ending it brings the best kind of happy.
kurals.university: The couplet is a chiasmus of superlatives: inbaththul inbam (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், joy among joys) answers thunbaththul thunbam (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம், sorrow among sorrows). The verb payakkum (பயக்கும், yields, produces) makes joy the direct fruit of hostility’s destruction (kedin, கெடின், ‘if it perishes’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it straightforwardly as ‘the greatest misery gone, the greatest delight comes’. The same formula ‘துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் கெடின்’ appears in Kural 369 on desire (avaa), so Valluvar ranks hostility alongside craving as the chief sources of suffering. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not connected with the Supreme ... can have neither transcendental intelligence nor a steady mind, without which there is no possibility of peace. And how can there be any happiness without peace?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna argues that real happiness depends on inner peace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: once the turmoil of hostility ends, the greatest joy follows.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Excerpt; links peace and happiness generally, not hostility specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus declares a special blessedness for those who end enmity.
christianity.tie_back: Both promise the highest happiness to those who end hostility.
christianity._accuracy_note: Blessedness rather than joy, and focused on making peace between others.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not hate one another, and do not be jealous of one another, and do not desert each other, and O, Allah's worshipers! Be brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet forbids mutual hatred and calls believers to live as brothers.
islam.tie_back: Brotherhood in place of hatred is the joy the Kural describes.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the call to drop hatred; the joy it brings is implied rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist celebrates the sweetness of people living together without strife.
judaism.tie_back: This is the ‘joy among joys’ that follows when hostility is gone.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the pleasure of harmony.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, friendly amidst the hostile. Amidst hostile men we dwell free from hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the happiness of those who stay free of hatred even among enemies.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts tie the highest happiness to freedom from hostility.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the end of the Odyssey, Athena halts the feud between Odysseus and the kinsmen of the slain suitors, and Zeus wills that they make a solemn peace so that friendship, wealth and peace may return to Ithaca.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic ends not with victory but with the end of a blood feud and the return of prosperity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The poem’s happy ending is precisely the end of hostility the Kural praises.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; peace is imposed by the gods rather than freely chosen.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza writes that one who seeks to overcome hatred with love fights joyfully and confidently, while one who avenges wrongs with reciprocal hatred lives in misery.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, answering hatred with love is itself a source of joy.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise links ending hostility to the highest delight.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics IV, Prop. 46 and Scholium

kurals.tamil:
இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை யாரே
மிக்லூக்கும் தன்மை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikaledhir saaindhozhuka vallaarai yaare
mikalookkum thanmai yavar.
kurals.meaning: Who could ever hope to overcome those who are able to turn away from hostility whenever it rises in them?
kurals.elementary: Picture someone trying to start a fight with a kid who just smiles and won’t fight back. After a while, there is nothing to fight about, and the bully gives up. The poet says nobody can beat a person who never lets anger take over.
kurals.university: The key phrase is ikal edhir saaindhu ozhuga (இகல் எதிர் சாய்ந்து ஒழுக): to ‘lean away against’ hostility, i.e. to recoil from it and conduct oneself in the opposite direction when it arises within. Puliyur Kesigan specifies ‘when hostility arises in one’s own heart’, so the victory is first over oneself; mikal ūkkum (to aspire to overcome) then describes would-be conquerors, of whom ‘who’ (yaare) implies none. Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the second line as ‘மிக்லூக்கும்’ while their own romanizations read ‘mikalookkum’ and thirukkural.net’s song version prints ‘மிகலூக்கும்’; the word is mikal + ūkkum, and the printed form appears to be a shared digital orthographic slip. The same form recurs in 858. The text is otherwise identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Before giving up this present body, if one is able to tolerate the urges of the material senses and check the force of desire and anger, he is well situated and is happy in this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the one who can check the force of anger becomes steady and secure.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural calls such a person unconquerable.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on mastering anger; ‘well situated’ rather than ‘invincible’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says the way to win against evil is not to be dragged into it but to answer with good.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes refusal of hostility the secret of being unconquered.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength as mastery over one’s own anger.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s unconquerable person is exactly this kind of strong one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city.’”
judaism.explanation: The sage Ben Zoma defines true might as self-mastery, quoting Proverbs on slowness to anger.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts place real power in conquering one’s own hostility.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria), citing Proverbs 16:32
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; excerpted from a longer mishnah.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that non-anger is itself the means of victory.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s unconquerable person wins by the same non-anger.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the North Wind and the Sun, the Wind blows harder and harder but cannot strip a traveller of his cloak, while the Sun’s gentle warmth makes him take it off.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gentleness succeeds where force and aggression fail.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the one who refuses hostility cannot be overcome.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The North Wind and the Sun (Townsend tr.)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Greek fable rather than myth, and about persuasion more than invincibility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius writes that kindness is invincible if it is genuine, since even the most insolent person can do nothing to one who stays kind and gently corrects him.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor holds that sincere goodwill disarms every attacker.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘who could overcome them?’ makes the same claim.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a near-identical claim.

kurals.tamil:
இகலின் மிகலினிது என்பவன் வாழ்க்கை
தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikalin mikalinidhu enbavan vaazhkkai
thavalum kedalum naniththu.
kurals.meaning: For the one who says it is sweet to get ahead through hostility, failure and ruin are close at hand.
kurals.elementary: Some people enjoy picking fights because winning feels good. But someone who always looks for a fight soon has no friends and lots of enemies, and things start to go wrong fast. The poet warns that loving fights leads to falling down.
kurals.university: Ikalin mikal inidhu (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது): ‘to excel (mikal) by means of hostility is sweet’ is the boast of the quarrelsome man. Valluvar answers that for him thavalum (தவலும், failing, slipping) and kedalum (கெடலும், perishing) are naniththu (நணித்து, near). Puliyur Kesigan reads mikal as ‘exceeding others in hostility’, Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘victory through hostility’, and Kalaignar as ‘thinking victory easy through opposition’. Pappaiah gives a distinctive reading: such a life’s survival is brief, and its ruin also comes within a brief time. The couplet turns from the inner disease to its social consequence. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, Shishupala heaps insult after insult on Krishna at Yudhishthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice, delighting in his hostility, until Krishna, having forborne a hundred offences, slays him in the assembly.
hinduism.explanation: A king who revelled in hostility met swift destruction.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man who found hostility sweet and found ruin near.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; fits the pattern closely.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a community that feeds on infighting will consume itself.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts warn that relish for hostility ends in self-destruction.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in consequence; addresses a community rather than an individual.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that quarrelling saps courage and makes strength vanish.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly says hostility brings swift failure.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on quarrelling leading to loss of strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells of a host who, out of personal hatred, threw a man named Bar Kamsa out of his feast; the humiliated guest’s revenge set in motion events the sages connect with the destruction of Jerusalem.
judaism.explanation: A private grudge, enjoyed and indulged, escalated into national catastrophe.
judaism.tie_back: This shows how near ruin is to those who indulge hostility.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; the Talmud also blames the sages’ passivity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that winning by conflict only breeds more enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise exposes the sweetness of victory through hostility as a trap.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the false sweetness of victory.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 18, after Patroclus dies because of his quarrel with Agamemnon, Achilles wishes that strife would perish from gods and men, along with the anger that grows sweeter than honey in a man’s heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles recognises too late that the sweetness of his anger brought ruin on those he loved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning: hostility tastes sweet, but ruin is near.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; striking match on hostility felt as sweet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Thucydides describes how, during the civil strife at Corcyra, factions came to prize revenge over self-preservation and admired the violent, until the whole Greek world was convulsed and its character corrupted.
philosophy.explanation: The historian shows that a culture which comes to love conflict quickly destroys itself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural states the same law for a single life.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 3.82-83

kurals.tamil:
மிகல்மேவல் மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார் இகல்மேவல்
இன்னா அறிவி னவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mikalmeval meypporul kaanaar ikalmeval
innaa arivi navar.
kurals.meaning: Those whose harmful minds are bent on hostility can never see the true principle that leads to success.
kurals.elementary: When you are really angry at someone, it is hard to think clearly, a bit like trying to read with foggy glasses. The poet says people who love fighting have foggy minds, so they miss the smart, true way to win.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two uses of mēval (மேவல், attaching to, desiring): ikal mēval (attachment to hostility) and mikal mēval (attaining victory). Those with innaa arivu (இன்னா அறிவு, a harmful or grievous intellect) who cling to hostility cannot see meypporul (மெய்ப்பொருள், the true substance or principle) of success. Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify this ‘true substance’ with nīti nūl porul, the teaching of the treatises on statecraft, so hostility blinds a ruler to sound policy; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more generally as ‘the truth that leads to victory’. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead splits the couplet into two statements about pride and hostility. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain from anger to delusion to the loss of discernment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural describes the endpoint: a mind given to hostility cannot see the truth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on hostility destroying discernment.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth, because that darkness hath blinded his eyes.”
christianity.explanation: John says that hatred blinds a person so that he cannot see his own way.
christianity.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s claim that hostility hides the true path.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that hatred can derail one’s sense of justice.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see hostility as distorting judgement.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on hatred distorting judgement; the Kural speaks of success rather than justice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s brothers, consumed by hatred, could no longer even speak to him calmly, and went on to sell him.
judaism.tie_back: Their story shows how hostility clouds judgement, the Kural’s point.
judaism._accuracy_note: Illustrative only; the verse shows hatred’s effect on speech, not explicitly on understanding.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who mistake the unessential to be essential and the essential to be unessential, dwelling in wrong thoughts, never arrive at the essential.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that minds caught in wrong thoughts never reach what truly matters.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says hostile minds never see the meypporul, the essential truth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘missing the essential’ idea; hostility is not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Ajax, the hero, consumed by resentment after Achilles’ armour is awarded to Odysseus, sets out to kill the Greek leaders, but Athena clouds his mind and he slaughters cattle instead, believing them his enemies.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax’s grudge literally makes him unable to see what is in front of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a vivid image of a hostile mind blind to reality.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; the blinding is attributed to Athena.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that when someone provokes you, it is your own judgement that has provoked you, and urges us not to be carried away by the first impression so as to gain time to see clearly.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, clear perception requires refusing to be seized by hostile impressions.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says hostility prevents one from seeing the truth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; focus is on judgement, not on success.

kurals.tamil:
இகலிற்கு எதிர்சாய்தல் ஆக்கம் அதனை
மிக்லூக்கின் ஊக்குமாம் கேடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikalirku edhirsaaidhal aakkam adhanai
mikalookkin ookkumaam kedu.
kurals.meaning: Turning away from hostility brings prosperity; whoever pushes it further invites ruin to hurry toward him.
kurals.elementary: A small fire can be stamped out, but if you keep feeding it sticks it grows until it burns the house. The poet says anger is like that: put it out and good things grow, feed it and trouble comes running.
kurals.university: The first line repeats the key verb of 855, edhir saaidhal (எதிர் சாய்தல், to lean away from), now naming its reward: aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity, growth). The second line plays on ūkkam (ஊக்கம், urging, zeal): if one urges hostility on (mikal ūkkin), ruin ‘urges itself’ (ūkkumaam kēdu) toward that person, an elegant mirroring. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line as checking hostility before it rises in one’s own heart; Pappaiah as ‘not welcoming’ it; Kalaignar as confronting and removing it. Textual note: as in 855, both base sources print ‘மிக்லூக்கின்’ while ytamizh romanizes ‘miklookkin’; the morphology is mikal + ūkkin, and the printed cluster looks like a shared digital slip. Otherwise identical.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names anger as one of three doors to ruin and urges renouncing it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says giving up hostility brings gain, while feeding it brings ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on anger leading to ruin; the gain side is implied.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that peace is the soil from which good fruit grows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says turning away from hostility yields prosperity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the positive half; the ruin half is not in this verse.

islam.quote_or_event: Muslims are urged not to cut off a brother for more than three days and to restrain anger, since the Prophet taught that ‘the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger’; the tradition treats unchecked quarrel as self-harming.
islam.explanation: Islamic ethics sets limits on how long estrangement may be fed.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats nursing hostility as harmful and checking it as beneficial.
islam._accuracy_note: Composite summary; no single text states the gain/ruin contrast.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises reward to the one who meets an enemy with kindness instead of hostility.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says turning from hostility brings gain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on reward for not feeding enmity; ruin side absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a mind turned toward hatred hurts its owner more than any enemy could.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s second line: feed hostility and ruin comes to you.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Seven Against Thebes, the brothers Eteocles and Polynices, cursed by their father and unwilling to yield, nurse their quarrel over the throne until they kill each other at the seventh gate.
greek_mythology.explanation: Neither brother would turn away from hostility, and both were destroyed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They embody the Kural’s warning that whoever urges hostility on is met by ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; inherited curse adds a fate element.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that hatred is increased by being returned, and can on the other hand be destroyed by love.
philosophy.explanation: Feeding hatred makes it grow; meeting it with love dissolves it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same two-way law the Kural states.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a near-identical principle.

kurals.tamil:
இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால் அதனை
மிகல்காணும் கேடு தரற்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikalkaanaan aakkam varungaal adhanai
mikalkaanum kedu thararku.
kurals.meaning: When good fortune is coming, a person does not think of hostility; when he is bringing ruin on himself, he looks to magnify it.
kurals.elementary: When you are having a great day, a small bump does not bother you. But on a bad day, you might turn a tiny bump into a huge fight that makes everything worse. The poet says growing a quarrel is a sign that trouble is on its way.
kurals.university: The couplet reads hostility as a symptom of one’s turning fortune. Ikal kaanaan (இகல் காணான், ‘does not regard hostility’) when aakkam (prosperity) is coming; but to bring on kēdu (கேடு, ruin) he mikal kaanum (மிகல் காணும், ‘sees its increase’, magnifies it). Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah add that the fortunate man ignores hostility even with cause, while the one heading for ruin seeks it even without cause. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mikal as ‘seeking to win against it’. The underlying idea, that a mind inclines toward quarrel when its own fall is approaching, resembles the Sanskrit maxim vināśa-kāle viparīta-buddhi (‘at the time of ruin the mind turns perverse’), though Valluvar states it without fatalism. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, Krishna travels to Hastinapura as envoy and offers Duryodhana peace for as little as five villages for the Pandavas; Duryodhana, on the brink of disaster, rejects every counsel of peace and even tries to seize Krishna, choosing the war that destroys his line.
hinduism.explanation: On the eve of ruin, Duryodhana magnifies the quarrel instead of ending it.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man who ‘looks to its increase’ when bringing ruin on himself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that choosing to escalate conflict leads to one’s own destruction.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly ties the escalation of hostility to self-made ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the escalation-to-ruin link; lacks the Kural’s point about fortune.

islam.quote_or_event: “Shall I not inform you of what is more virtuous than the rank of fasting, Salat, and charity? ... Making peace between each other. For indeed spoiling relations with each other is the Haliqah.”
islam.explanation: The hadith calls the corruption of relationships ‘the shaver’, something that strips away what one has.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats magnifying discord as a mark and cause of ruin.
islam._accuracy_note: Excerpt; graded Da'if by Darussalam on sunnah.com though Tirmidhi called it sahih.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the Second Temple was destroyed, although its generation studied Torah and did good deeds, because of baseless hatred (sinat chinam), which it weighs as equal to idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed together.
judaism.explanation: A society on the verge of catastrophe was marked by unprovoked hatred.
judaism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural: hostility without cause accompanies approaching ruin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; collective and historical rather than personal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a corrupted mind brings suffering after it as surely as a cart follows an ox.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly sees the turn toward hostility as the mind bringing its own ruin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: General law of mind and consequence; hostility not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Antigone, the Chorus recalls the ancient saying that evil comes to seem good to the one whose mind a god is leading toward ruin, as Creon stubbornly hardens his quarrel with Antigone and Haemon.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks saw stubborn, worsening quarrel as a sign that doom was near.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s observation that ruin-bound minds magnify hostility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the Greek frames it as divine leading.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens On Anger by describing anger as heedless of itself, eager to harm another, rushing onto weapons and greedy for a vengeance that drags the avenger down with it.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca portrays hostile passion as a drive toward one’s own destruction.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly sees magnified hostility as the means by which a person brings on ruin.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of the opening description.

kurals.tamil:
இகலானாம் இன்னாத எல்லாம் நகலானாம்
நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikalaanaam innaadha ellaam nakalaanaam
nannayam ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: From hostility come all painful things; from friendliness comes the proud wealth called true goodness.
kurals.elementary: Grumpy, fighting groups have lots of problems, while friendly groups share, help, and feel proud of each other. The poet ends the chapter simply: fighting brings every kind of trouble, and friendship brings goodness you can be proud of.
kurals.university: The closing couplet sets ikal against nakal (நகல், literally ‘laughing together’, hence friendship, cordiality). From ikal come innaadha ellaam (இன்னாத எல்லாம், all that is painful); from nakal comes nannayam ennum serukku (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு), ‘the elation called great good’. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss nannayam as nalla nīti (good justice or policy) and serukku as perumidha nilai (a state of dignified pride); Pappaiah renders it ‘the wealth-pride of justice’, while Kalaignar reads it as ‘great joy’. Serukku usually means arrogance in the Kural, so its positive use here is notable: the only pride worth having is the dignity friendship confers. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The closing hymn of the Rig Veda (10.191, the Samjñāna Sūkta) calls on people to assemble together, speak together, and let their minds and purposes be in harmony, so that they may dwell well together.
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic tradition ends its oldest collection with a prayer for concord.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s close, it names unity of heart as the source of all good.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the hymn praises concord but does not state the contrast with hostility.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that strife is the breeding ground of every kind of evil.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first line almost exactly: from hostility comes everything painful.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close to the first half; the next verses (3:17-18) give the peace half.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that answering evil with good turns an enemy into a devoted friend.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise sets enmity’s harms against friendship’s goodness.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: enmity transformed into friendship as the better path.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hillel used to say: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind and drawing them close to the Torah.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel holds up Aaron, the peacemaker, as the model to follow.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s closing praise of friendliness matches this ideal of loving peace and people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the positive half; the harms of hostility are not stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a pure, well-disposed mind brings happiness that never leaves.
buddhism.tie_back: Paired with verse 1, it mirrors the Kural’s two paths: hostility brings pain, goodwill brings good.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the two-path structure; friendship is not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But abhorred Strife bare painful Toil and Forgetfulness and Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings also, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin, all of one nature.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod makes Strife (Eris) the mother of nearly every human misery.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first line as a genealogy: all painful things are born of hostility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the first half.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes concord (homonoia) as political friendship: citizens of one mind about their common interests, which good people achieve and bad people cannot, since they are always seeking advantage and so fall into faction.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, friendship between citizens is the foundation of a good city, and faction its ruin.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly closes by setting friendship’s goodness against hostility’s harms.
